DUTY TO MITIGATE DAMAGES AFTER WRONGFUL DISCHARGE (CIV. CODE § 3300; PARKER V. TWENTIETH CENTURY-FOX; CACI NO. 3963) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

DUTY TO MITIGATE DAMAGES AFTER WRONGFUL DISCHARGE — APPLICABILITY NOTE
This information sheet concerns Jordan Lee's former position as Regional Sales Manager with Acme, Inc., recorded here as having ended on August 28, 2026. It describes what California's Civil Code, the California Supreme Court's decision in Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp. (1970), later Court of Appeal decisions, and the Judicial Council's civil jury instructions say about how a wrongfully discharged employee's lost-earnings damages are measured and reduced: the employer's burden to prove that damages could have been avoided, the "comparable or substantially similar" employment standard, the treatment of earnings the employee actually received from other work, the consequence of losing a replacement job, the exclusion of unemployment insurance and similar collateral-source benefits from the offset, self-employment as mitigation, and who decides these questions. Whether Acme, Inc.'s termination of Jordan Lee was wrongful in any sense, whether any other employment was available to Jordan Lee after August 28, 2026, what Jordan Lee earned or could have earned, and whether any offset applies are facts this sheet does not determine. Naming the parties and dates here does not itself establish that any of the rules described below applies to their separation, and this sheet states what the statute, the courts, and the jury instructions say rather than advising anyone what to do about a particular claim or defense.

THE STARTING POINT: CONTRACT DAMAGES UNDER CIVIL CODE SECTION 3300 AND THE PARKER MEASURE OF RECOVERY FOR A WRONGFULLY DISCHARGED EMPLOYEE
Civil Code section 3300 supplies the general measure of damages for breach of a contract: the amount that will compensate the aggrieved party for all the detriment proximately caused by the breach, or that would be likely to result from it in the ordinary course of things, except where the Code expressly provides otherwise. In Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp. (1970), the California Supreme Court stated how that measure is applied when the contract broken is one of employment and the employee has been wrongfully discharged: the recovery is the amount of salary agreed upon for the period of service, less the amount that the employer affirmatively proves the employee has earned, or with reasonable effort might have earned, from other employment. The rule therefore has two parts — a gross figure fixed by the agreed compensation for the unexpired period, and a deduction that exists only to the extent the employer proves it. As applied to Jordan Lee's former position as Regional Sales Manager with Acme, Inc., this clause states the formula the courts use; what the agreed compensation was, what period remained, and what (if anything) was earned or could have been earned elsewhere after August 28, 2026 are facts this clause does not determine.

  — Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp. (1970) 3 Cal.3d 176, 3 Cal.3d 176, 181 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1453074/parker-v-twentieth-century-fox-film-corp/)

  — Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox Film Corp. (1970) 3 Cal.3d 176, 3 Cal.3d 176, 179 (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1453074/parker-v-twentieth-century-fox-film-corp/)
  Known gap: This clause pairs the Civil Code's general contract-damages measure with the Supreme Court's employment-specific formulation in Parker. Parker was a breach-of-contract action on a written fixed-term contract (a $750,000 guaranteed fee for a motion picture); the same mitigation formula has since been applied by California courts to wrongful-termination claims sounding in tort and under the Fair Employment and Housing Act (see the later clauses citing Mize-Kurzman, Cordero-Sacks, and the CACI Directions for Use), but Parker itself did not address those claims. The clause does not address how future (front-pay) losses are reduced to present value, the period over which employment was reasonably certain to continue, non-economic damages, or any statutory remedy that displaces the contract measure. FAILURE TO MITIGATE IS AN AFFIRMATIVE DEFENSE THE EMPLOYER MUST PROVE: THE THREE ELEMENTS IN CACI NO. 3963
The deduction described in the preceding clause is not automatic. Parker frames it as an amount the employer "affirmatively proves," and the Court of Appeal in Mize-Kurzman v. Marin Community College Dist. (2012) restated the point directly: it is the employer's burden to affirmatively prove failure to mitigate as an affirmative defense. Mize-Kurzman also described the underlying doctrine — the common-law rule of avoidable consequences, under which a person injured by another's wrongful conduct is not compensated for damages that could have been avoided by reasonable effort or expenditure — and noted, quoting an earlier decision, that both public and private employees faced with a wrongful discharge have a legal duty to mitigate damages while pursuing remedies against their former employer. The Judicial Council's civil jury instruction on the defense, CACI No. 3963, tells jurors that the employer must prove all three of the following: that employment substantially similar to the plaintiff's former job was available; that the plaintiff failed to make reasonable efforts to seek (and, where the evidence supports it, retain) that employment; and the amount the plaintiff could have earned from it. The Sources and Authority for the companion instruction CACI No. 3961 add, quoting Powerhouse Motorsports Group, Inc. v. Yamaha Motor Corp., U.S.A. (2013), that whether a plaintiff acted reasonably to mitigate is a factual matter for the trier of fact and that the burden of proving a failure to mitigate is on the defendant, not the other way around. Whether Acme, Inc. could carry that burden as to Jordan Lee's job search after August 28, 2026 is a question of evidence this clause does not resolve.

ONLY “COMPARABLE, OR SUBSTANTIALLY SIMILAR” EMPLOYMENT COUNTS: THE EMPLOYEE NEED NOT SEEK OR ACCEPT DIFFERENT OR INFERIOR WORK
Parker attaches a condition to the deduction for earnings the employee did not actually receive: before projected earnings from other employment opportunities that the discharged employee did not seek or accept can be applied in mitigation, the employer must show that the other employment was comparable, or substantially similar, to the employment of which the employee was deprived. The employee's rejection of, or failure to seek, other available employment of a different or inferior kind may not be used to reduce damages. The court added that no case it had found treats the reasonableness of the employee's refusal as part of that analysis: reasonableness is not an element of a wrongfully discharged employee's option to reject, or fail to seek, different or inferior employment. CACI No. 3963 converts the standard into a list of factors for the jury to weigh in deciding whether other employment was substantially similar — whether the nature of the work was different, whether the new position was substantially inferior, whether the salary, benefits, and hours were similar, whether similar skills, background, and experience were required, whether the job responsibilities were similar, and whether the job was in the same locality — with room for other relevant factors shown by the evidence. The Court of Appeal in Villacorta v. Cemex Cement, Inc. (2013) treated the location of the new job as one of the factors bearing on whether it is inferior, where the replacement position required the employee to live away from his family during the work week. Whether any position available to Jordan Lee after August 28, 2026 was substantially similar to the Regional Sales Manager position at Acme, Inc. is a question this clause does not answer.

HOW PARKER APPLIED THE STANDARD: “BLOOMER GIRL” VERSUS “BIG COUNTRY, BIG MAN,” AND WHY LOSS OF CONTRACT RIGHTS MADE THE SUBSTITUTE OFFER INFERIOR
The facts of Parker illustrate what “different or inferior” means. The actress Shirley MacLaine Parker had contracted to play the female lead in a musical, “Bloomer Girl,” to be filmed in Los Angeles. The studio cancelled the picture and, in the same letter, offered her the lead in a dramatic western, “Big Country, Big Man,” to be filmed in Australia, at identical compensation but without the director and screenplay approval rights the original contract had given her. She declined, sued for the guaranteed compensation, and obtained summary judgment; the studio's only defense was that her refusal of the substitute role was an unreasonable failure to mitigate. The Supreme Court held that the offer could not be applied in mitigation because it was of employment both different and inferior, and that no triable issue of fact existed on the point. The difference in kind, the court said, was demonstrated by the mere circumstance that one role called on her talents as a dancer and actress in a musical to be produced in Los Angeles while the other was a straight dramatic role in a western set in an opal mine in Australia; the female lead as a dramatic actress in a western could by no stretch of imagination be considered the equivalent of or substantially similar to the lead in a song-and-dance production. Separately, the elimination or impairment of the approval rights made the substitute offer inferior: no expertise or judicial notice is required, the court said, to hold that depriving an employee of rights held under the original employment contract converts the “other employment” relied on by the employer into inferior employment the employee need not seek or accept. This clause describes the decided case; it does not compare any position offered to or available to Jordan Lee with the Regional Sales Manager position at Acme, Inc.

EARNINGS THE EMPLOYEE ACTUALLY RECEIVED: RABAGO-ALVAREZ, AND THE VILLACORTA/MARTINEZ SPLIT OVER WAGES EARNED IN AN INFERIOR JOB
Parker's first sentence deducts what the employee "has earned" as well as what the employee "with reasonable effort might have earned"; its comparable-employment condition is stated only for the second category ("projected earnings from other employment opportunities not sought or accepted"). In Rabago-Alvarez v. Dart Industries, Inc. (1976), the employee conceded that her actual earnings from part-time work after her discharge were deductible, and the Court of Appeal deducted them; but it reversed the trial court's further deduction of amounts she supposedly could have earned in later years, because the record showed no comparable employment was available and the trial court had reasoned that by once accepting menial, inferior work she had waived her right to decline such work in the future — a theory the court said was supported neither by California decisional law nor by basic principles of fairness, since it would senselessly penalize an employee who, from an honest desire to work or a lack of financial resources, takes whatever employment can be found. The Courts of Appeal have since divided over wages actually earned in an inferior job. Villacorta v. Cemex Cement, Inc. (2013) read Parker and Rabago-Alvarez to mean that if the new job is different or inferior, the wages from that job may not be used to mitigate damages, and upheld a lost-wage award that did not deduct the plaintiff's earnings from a higher-paid but distant replacement position. Martinez v. Rite Aid Corp. (2021) expressly disagreed, reasoning that Parker and Rabago-Alvarez address projected income and the employer's burden of proof, not amounts actually received, and held that although an employee may not be obliged to accept inferior employment, if the employee accepts employment and receives earnings, those actual earnings should be deducted from an award of past lost earnings; the court reduced the award by the $140,840 the plaintiff had earned after her discharge. The Judicial Council's Sources and Authority for CACI No. 3963 now cite both decisions. Which line of authority a court would follow as to any earnings Jordan Lee received after August 28, 2026 is a question this clause does not resolve.

LOSING THE REPLACEMENT JOB: STANCHFIELD AND THE “RETAIN” ELEMENT
The duty to mitigate is not exhausted by finding a comparable job. In Stanchfield v. Hamer Toyota, Inc. (1995), the wrongfully discharged employee found comparable employment within days but was then fired from it for cause. The Court of Appeal held that a jury, in deciding the reasonableness of a wrongfully discharged employee's efforts to mitigate, may properly take into account the employee's failure to retain comparable employment once it has been secured, because the employee's actual damage is the amount of money he or she was out of pocket by reason of the wrongful discharge; therefore, where the jury determines that the employee was fired from a substantially similar position for cause, any amount the employee with reasonable effort could have earned by retaining that employment is deducted from the damages that would otherwise have been awarded under the original employment agreement. The Judicial Council incorporated this holding into CACI No. 3963: the second element may be read as a failure to make reasonable efforts to seek "[and retain]" substantially similar employment, and an optional closing paragraph tells jurors that, in deciding whether the plaintiff failed to make reasonable efforts to retain comparable employment, they should consider whether the plaintiff quit or was discharged from that employment for a reason within the plaintiff's control. The Directions for Use state that this bracketed language is based on Stanchfield. Whether Jordan Lee obtained and then lost any comparable position after August 28, 2026, and if so why, are facts this clause does not determine.

WHAT IS NOT DEDUCTED: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE BENEFITS, RETIREMENT BENEFITS, AND AN OFFER TO CONTINUE AT LOWER PAY
The offset is for earnings from other employment, and California courts have declined to extend it to other money received during unemployment. In Billetter v. Posell (1949), the Court of Appeal held that payments the discharged employee received from the state unemployment compensation fund are not deductible as compensation received from other employment in mitigation of damages, because benefits of that character are intended to alleviate the distress of unemployment and not to diminish what the employer must pay as damages for the wrongful discharge. The actress Shirley MacLaine Parker had contracted to play the female lead in a musical, “Bloomer Girl,” to be filmed in Los Angeles. The studio cancelled the picture and, in the same letter, offered her the lead in a dramatic western, “Big Country, Big Man,” to be filmed in Australia, at identical compensation but without the director and screenplay approval rights the original contract had given her. She declined, sued for the guaranteed compensation, and obtained summary judgment; the studio's only defense was that her refusal of the substitute role was an unreasonable failure to mitigate. The difference in kind, the court said, was demonstrated by the mere circumstance that one role called on her talents as a dancer and actress in a musical to be produced in Los Angeles while the other was a straight dramatic role in a western set in an opal mine in Australia; the female lead as a dramatic actress in a western could by no stretch of imagination be considered the equivalent of or substantially similar to the lead in a song-and-dance production. Separately, the elimination or impairment of the approval rights made the substitute offer inferior: no expertise or judicial notice is required, the court said, to hold that depriving an employee of rights held under the original employment contract converts the “other employment” relied on by the employer into inferior employment the employee need not seek or accept. expectedJSON.body: The duty to mitigate is not exhausted by finding a comparable job. In Stanchfield v. Hamer Toyota, Inc. (1995), the wrongfully discharged employee found comparable employment within days but was then fired from it for cause. The Court of Appeal held that a jury, in deciding the reasonableness of a wrongfully discharged employee's efforts to mitigate, may properly take into account the employee's failure to retain comparable employment once it has been secured, because the employee's actual damage is the amount of money he or she was out of pocket by reason of the wrongful discharge; therefore, where the jury determines that the employee was fired from a substantially similar position for cause, any amount the employee with reasonable effort could have earned by retaining that employment is deducted from the damages that would otherwise have been awarded under the original employment agreement. The Judicial Council incorporated this holding into CACI No. 3963: the second element may be read as a failure to make reasonable efforts to seek "[and retain]" substantially similar employment, and an optional closing paragraph tells jurors that, in deciding whether the plaintiff failed to make reasonable efforts to retain comparable employment, they should consider whether the plaintiff quit or was discharged from that employment for a reason within the plaintiff's control. The Directions for Use state that this bracketed language is based on Stanchfield. Whether Jordan Lee obtained and then lost any comparable position after August 28, 2026, and if so why, are facts this clause does not determine.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the rule for a replacement job that was substantially similar to the original; Stanchfield's holding is expressly limited to that situation ("fired from a substantially similar position for cause"), and it does not say what happens when an employee loses a replacement job that was different or inferior, or loses a comparable job for reasons outside the employee's control. Stanchfield's "actual damage" sentence quotes Erler v. Five Points Motors, Inc. (1967) 249 Cal.App.2d 560, which was not fetched for this document; that sentence is paraphrased in the body rather than quoted. Stanchfield addressed a modification of the former standard instruction (BAJI No. 10.16); the CACI instruction quoted here post-dates and incorporates it. expectedJSON.body: The offset is for earnings from other employment, and California courts have declined to extend it to other money received during unemployment. In Billetter v. Posell (1949), the Court of Appeal held that payments the discharged employee received from the state unemployment compensation fund are not deductible as compensation received from other employment in mitigation of damages, because benefits of that character are intended to alleviate the distress of unemployment and not to diminish what the employer must pay as damages for the wrongful discharge. Rabago-Alvarez restated the same rule, and Mize-Kurzman v. Marin Community College Dist. (2012) traced it through Monroe v. Oakland Unified School Dist. (1981), quoting Monroe's statement that the law of this state does not require the mitigation of damages by everything of value received during a period of wrongful unemployment — the rule of mitigation requires only the duty to seek other employment. Mize-Kurzman applied the same reasoning to retirement benefits: it held that the trial court erred in admitting evidence of the employee's eligibility to retire and her projected pension on the issue of mitigation, explaining that had she actually retired and taken her pension the court would have been required to exclude the evidence as a collateral source, and that it made little sense to admit evidence of benefits she never received when the same evidence would have been precluded had she received them. Billetter also addressed the employer's own offer to keep the employee on at reduced pay: an employee is not required to perform the same work for a lesser price in mitigation of damages, and an offer by the employer that wrongfully discharged the employee to continue the employment at a lower rate of wages is not a defense. Whether Jordan Lee received unemployment insurance, retirement, or similar benefits after leaving Acme, Inc., and whether Acme, Inc. offered continued employment at lower pay, are facts this clause does not determine.

Benefits of this character are intended to alleviate the distress of unemployment and not to diminish the amount which an employer must pay as damages for the wrongful discharge of an employee.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause states the collateral-source treatment the cited cases gave to unemployment insurance benefits, retirement benefits, and an employer's reduced-wage offer; it does not catalogue every benefit that might be received after a discharge. Mize-Kurzman itself noted that disability benefits were deducted in Mayer v. Multistate Legal Studies, Inc. (1997) 52 Cal.App.4th 1428 only because the employee there conceded the point, and that the collateral source rule generally does not apply when the benefit payment comes from the employer itself; the treatment of severance pay, employer-funded disability plans, or other employer-sourced payments is not addressed here. The Billetter reduced-wage holding concerned an offer made at the time of termination to continue at lower pay; it does not address an employer's later offer of reinstatement on the original terms. Monroe and Mayer were not independently fetched and are described only as Mize-Kurzman characterized them. Mize-Kurzman's spelling “deductable” is the opinion's own and is reproduced as found.

expectedJSON.body: Three further points round out the doctrine. First, starting a business can satisfy the duty to mitigate. In Cordero-Sacks v. Housing Authority of City of Los Angeles (2011), a discharged attorney who opened her own modestly successful practice defeated the employer's mitigation defense; the Court of Appeal, discussing federal authority, stated that self-employment is not unreasonable mitigation as long as the discharged employee applies sufficient effort trying to make the business successful, even if those efforts fail, and it upheld the trial court's refusal of the employer's proposed instruction that would have required the jury first to find self-employment reasonable and to treat an unprofitable business as a reason to resume the job search. Second, the defense is not confined to contract claims: the Directions for Use for CACI No. 3963 state that the instruction may be given for any claim in which the plaintiff seeks past and future lost earnings from an employer for a wrongful termination — for example, termination in violation of public policy or under the Fair Employment and Housing Act — when there is evidence that the damages could have been mitigated. Third, who decides. The Judicial Council's Sources and Authority quote California School Employees Assn. v. Personnel Commission (1973) for the observation that there is some authority treating whether other employment is comparable or substantially similar as a question of fact, while the issue of substantial similarity or inferiority has often been decided as a matter of law in California; Parker itself resolved the question on summary judgment, and Villacorta and Cordero-Sacks left it to juries. Whether Jordan Lee's activities after August 28, 2026 — including any self-employment — amounted to reasonable mitigation, and whether the comparison to the Regional Sales Manager position at Acme, Inc. would be resolved by a judge or a jury, are questions this clause does not answer.

The Cordero-Sacks sentence on self-employment is the Court of Appeal's own summary of a Seventh Circuit decision (Smith v. Great American Restaurants, Inc. The CACI Directions for Use describe when the instruction may be given; they are not themselves a holding that mitigation applies identically to every statutory claim, and this document does not address statutes that supply their own back-pay rules.
